title: Agile Release Planning That Bends Without Breaking
summary: Notes from Mike Cohn's Agile Estimating and Planning: rank work by value and risk, slice stories thin, keep a visible cut line and report scope growth honestly.
author: Nguyen Le Phong

book.title: Agile Estimating and Planning
book.note: This article is a personal reflection from the book, focused on release planning, prioritization, buffers, and communication. It is not a chapter-by-chapter summary.

html:
Week ten of a twelve-week release. The payment partner's sandbox finally works, two weeks later than promised. Someone opens the plan and asks the question nobody wants to ask: "So what do we cut?" If the plan has no answer, the next hour turns into a negotiation between tired people. If the plan already has a line through it, with "must ship" above and "nice if we get there" below, the same question takes five minutes.

This post is about drawing that line early, and about everything that has to be true for it to work. It's my second set of notes from Mike Cohn's Agile Estimating and Planning. The first one covered estimates. This one covers release planning: what goes first, how to slice stories, where the slack lives and how to talk about a plan that keeps moving.

Book source

Mike Cohn, Agile Estimating and Planning, Prentice Hall, 2005 (book page). Chapter numbers below follow the publisher's table of contents. The product examples and their numbers are made-up scenarios. The numbers I attribute to Cohn come from the book.

Planning is a search for value

Chapter 1, "The Purpose of Planning," has the line that frames the whole book: planning, especially the ongoing, iterative kind, "is a quest for value." The question underneath every plan is "What should we build?", and Cohn says you can't answer it all at once. You might start out planning a feature set for August 31. In June you learn something and decide that a slightly later date with a bit more is the better deal, or a slightly earlier date with a bit less. A plan that can't make that trade is a schedule wearing a plan's clothes.

Most backlogs aren't ordered by value, though. They're ordered by whoever asked loudest, whatever looks easiest, or whatever the team finds interesting this month. Chapter 9, "Prioritizing Themes," offers four factors to use instead:

  • the financial value of having the feature,
  • the cost of building it (and maybe supporting it),
  • how much useful learning and new knowledge building it creates,
  • how much risk building it removes.

Mountain Goat Software's newer writing adds a fifth factor, dependencies, for items that unblock other work (5 key factors for backlog prioritization).

Here's how that looks with three candidates on the table: a new sales dashboard, a billing reconciliation tool and an onboarding redesign. Say the dashboard makes demos nicer but won't bring in revenue soon. Reconciliation would save finance a few hours of manual matching every week and stop them pinging engineers to read logs. And nobody knows why so many signups stall at email verification, so the onboarding work is mostly about learning. Write one value line per candidate like that, and the priority meeting stops being a debate about taste.

Let risk pull work forward

Value alone doesn't settle the order. Chapter 9 crosses value with risk and gets four quadrants: high value and high risk, do first. High value and low risk, do second. Low value and low risk, do last. Low value and high risk, avoid, ideally right out of the project. Cohn sums it up as "work first on high-value features but use risk as a tie-breaker."

The reason risky work goes early is simple. If it's going to fail, you want to find out while there's still room to change course. Say your customers keep asking for a new e-wallet payment option. Value is high. Risk is high too: the partner is new to you, callbacks may arrive late, the reconciliation rules are fuzzy and support has no playbook for failed payments. Leave it for the last month and you'll meet those risks with zero room to react. Ship a thin slice early instead, like test top-ups for internal staff only, and you learn the API, the ops side and the support flow while the release can still bend.

Work typeExampleWhat Cohn suggests
High value, high riskNew payment partner, unfamiliar fraud rules, unclear compliance path.Do first, while you still have time to act on what you learn.
High value, low riskA much-requested export built on known data and a known UI pattern.Do second. Same value, fewer surprises, so it can wait a bit.
Low value, low riskA nice-to-have setting with little evidence anyone will use it.Do last. Dropping it costs little, which makes it a good buffer candidate.
Low value, high riskAn experiment with unclear users that would reshape the architecture.Avoid. Push it out of the release, or shrink it to a tiny discovery spike.

Chapter 11, "Prioritizing Desirability," adds the Kano model. Threshold features (must-haves) have to be there for the product to succeed at all, and making them better barely moves satisfaction. Linear features follow "the more, the better." Exciters and delighters are the ones users didn't know to ask for. Cohn's order: every threshold feature has to be there before release, though not necessarily in the first iterations, and a partial version is sometimes enough. His example is FrameMaker offering just one level of undo, which moved him a long way up the satisfaction curve, even though he'd have liked more. After that, fit in as many linear features as you can, and then, time permitting, a few delighters.

Take an English-learning app. Lessons that load, progress that saves and audio that plays are threshold. More practice sets and faster feedback on answers are linear. A small hint after you miss the same sound three times might be a delighter. If the team spends three sprints polishing screen transitions while progress still gets lost now and then, it's decorating a house with a leaky roof.

Slice stories so every slice works

Chapter 12, "Splitting User Stories," is the most hands-on part of the book. A story needs splitting when it won't fit in an iteration, when you can't estimate it with any confidence, or when it hides several priorities in one sentence. Cohn lists the cuts that usually work:

  • by the data it handles (one card type first, the rest later),
  • by operation (create and read now, update and delete next),
  • by pulling out a cross-cutting concern like security, logging or error handling into its own story,
  • by separating the performance target from the working feature,
  • by priority, when parts of the story matter more than others.

And the cut that doesn't work: splitting into tasks like "code the UI" and "write the middle tier." Cohn borrows Hunt and Thomas's idea from The Pragmatic Programmer and says to fire a tracer bullet through the story instead: a thin slice that goes through every layer, with a bit of UI, a bit of middle tier and a bit of database. He also warns against "the temptation of related changes," those extra fixes you slip in because you're in that file anyway. For two-week iterations he suggests stories of roughly two to five days.

Story too largeA first slice you can learn fromWhat the team learns
Manage payment methodsAdd one card type in one region, with basic validation.Whether the form, tokenization, API and validation errors work end to end.
Full revenue reportingExport a CSV for one date range and one transaction type.Data source, permissions, time zones and rough performance.
Notification centerShow one notification type in the app, no filters or preferences yet.Event source, unread state and whether people actually read them.
A splitting question

Swap "Which technical tasks do we need?" for "What's the smallest thing a user can see that would reduce risk or teach us something?"

Splitting by priority is the one teams forget most. Cohn's example is a login story with three conditions: valid credentials get you in, three wrong passwords lock you out until you call support, and a lockout sends you an email. The product owner won't ship without the first one, but might ship without the other two. That's two stories, not one. Order notifications work the same way: the confirmation email is a must, push notifications are a should, branded templates are a could, and a full preference center can wait until people actually use the rest.

Say out loud which one is fixed

Chapter 13, "Release Planning Essentials," points out that a product owner usually brings targets for schedule, scope and resources, and one of them is almost always the boss. A date-driven project must ship by a certain date, and the feature set is negotiable. A feature-driven project needs a certain set of features, and you'd like it as soon as possible. A lot of planning pain comes from pretending both are fixed while also expecting quality to hold.

A tax-reporting change that becomes mandatory on July 1 is date-driven. The form, the export and the audit trail have to work by then, and a nicer dashboard can slip. Moving from an old billing system to a new one is usually feature-driven. If invoicing, payment retries and basic reconciliation aren't ready, switching over on a nice round date just hands the risk to the ops team.

So skip "Can we finish everything by the date?" Ask "Given this date, which scope is truly required, which is optional, and what news would make us replan?" That conversation is a lot less dramatic in week one than in week ten.

Buffers are part of the design

Uncertainty doesn't go away because a plan looks confident. You can hide it inside every task estimate, where nobody sees it, or put it in one visible place at the release level. Chapter 17, "Buffering Plans for Uncertainty," argues for the second and describes two kinds of buffer.

A feature buffer is the simpler one. The customer picks the work that's truly mandatory, then adds another 25 to 40 percent as optional, going toward the high end when uncertainty is higher. The optional work is built last. Cohn's example: 100 points of mandatory stories plus 30 optional points makes 130. At 10 points per one-week iteration, that's a 13-iteration plan where, if all goes well, the mandatory work is done after 10. He notes that DSDM's MoSCoW rules do something similar: in the version he describes, no more than 70 percent of planned effort can go to Must Haves.

A schedule buffer protects a date instead. You estimate each story twice, once at 50 percent confidence and once at 90 percent. The buffer is the square root of the sum of the squared gaps between the two, and Cohn says it should be at least 20 percent of the total project duration. The math matters less than the idea: the slack sits in one place everyone can see, instead of hiding in every estimate.

Here's a feature buffer in practice. In a 12-week checkout release, the must-haves are product selection, discount codes, payment, a confirmation email and order lookup for support. The shoulds are saved cards, voucher suggestions and a better transaction history. The coulds are animation, campaign themes and advanced filters. When the payment integration runs two weeks late, you cut from the bottom and still ship a checkout that works.

Then write the cut line where everyone reads it, such as the release note: "Release 1 must ship product selection, discount codes, payment, confirmation email and support lookup. Saved cards are below the cut line. Advanced filters are optional." One sentence like that saves you a surprise argument in week ten.

Track scope, not just speed

A normal release burndown shows remaining work going down. Chapter 19, "Monitoring the Release Plan," shows a version with bars that separates two things the line mixes up. The top of each bar drops as the team finishes work. The bottom drops below zero when work is added and rises when work is removed. Cohn's example: a 240-point release at an expected 30 points per iteration, so about eight iterations. After the first iteration the product owner adds 50 points, and the second bar runs from −50 to 210. Velocity is fine. The release just grew to 260 points.

That's a different conversation from "the team is slow." Pushing the team harder won't fix scope growth. Choosing which new scope replaces which old scope will.

Inside an iteration, Chapter 20 covers the task board, and its value is that it sits next to the work: blocked tasks, unverified work, stories that are "almost done" but not accepted. In Chapter 22, "Why Agile Planning Works," one of Cohn's reasons is that progress is measured at the team level, not the individual level. Once the board turns into a leaderboard, people stop putting bad news on it.

Chapter 21, "Communicating about Plans," asks for communication that's "frequent, honest, and two-way." Honest matters most. Cohn tells of a team whose executives asked for more work than could fit because "that way if they get 80%, they're happy," and once both sides play that game, nobody trusts the plan. He also shares the end-of-iteration summary he writes, which takes him under 30 minutes. A good update can be shorter still:

"This iteration we got 5 of 6 stories accepted. The CSV export slipped because data permissions were trickier than we assumed. Our last three iterations landed between 28 and 31 points. If the release date holds, advanced filters move out. If advanced filters stay, we need to reopen the date."

No drama, nothing hidden, and the decision lands with the person who owns it.

Try this week

  • Write one value line for each of your top five backlog items: money, cost, learning or risk removed.
  • Find the riskiest high-value item in your release and plan a thin, internal-only slice of it for the next iteration.
  • Take one big story and split it by priority, the way Cohn splits his login story.
  • Say out loud whether this release is date-driven or feature-driven, and write it at the top of the plan.
  • Draw the cut line and put it in the release note.
  • In your next update, report scope added next to work done.

Cohn's answer in Chapter 22 to why agile planning works has little to do with predicting the future. Plans get revisited often, they're built around features instead of tasks, and uncertainty gets planned for in the open. Write the plan, learn from the work, update the plan, say what changed. Repeat every iteration, even when it's a little uncomfortable.

faqs.q: What is release planning in Agile?
faqs.a: It's a plan for a longer stretch than one iteration, usually several, that decides what to build and roughly when. Mike Cohn calls planning a quest for value: you balance scope, schedule and resources, then revisit the plan every iteration as you learn.

faqs.q: How should a team prioritize work for a release?
faqs.a: Cohn's Agile Estimating and Planning (Chapter 9) weighs four factors: financial value, cost, the learning a feature creates and the risk it removes. Crossing value with risk gives an order: high value and high risk first, high value and low risk second, low value and low risk last, and avoid low value with high risk.

A slice of the release that's optional by design. In Chapter 17 the customer picks the mandatory work, then adds 25 to 40 percent more as optional work that's built last. With 100 mandatory points and 30 optional ones, the plan covers 130 points, and late surprises eat into the optional part first.

faqs.q: What's the difference between a date-driven and a feature-driven release?
faqs.a: A date-driven release must ship by a fixed date, so scope is what you negotiate. A feature-driven release must include a fixed set of features, so the date moves. Cohn's Chapter 13 asks teams to name which one they're in, since treating both as fixed is where plans break.

faqs.q: Why not split user stories into UI, API and database tasks?
faqs.a: Layer-by-layer tasks don't give you anything a user can see or a product owner can accept. Cohn's Chapter 12 suggests a tracer bullet instead: a thin slice through every layer that works end to end, plus splits by data, operation, cross-cutting concern, performance or priority.
